current_answer: A new French administrative-record study finds that permanent hires of 21–29-year-olds fell more in highly AI-exposed occupations than in less-exposed ones from November 2022 to March 2026; permanent-contract endings fell too. Anthropic reports a sharply smaller junior share of technical hires at its own growing firm. Neither study identifies how many jobs AI caused to disappear. Broad U.S. tracking still finds no clear economy-wide AI footprint, so the best-supported warning is concentrated entry friction, not proven mass unemployment.

catalogue_card.question: Are junior jobs already being cut by AI?
catalogue_card.text: French permanent hires of 21–29-year-olds fell 28.3% in the most AI-exposed occupations versus 7.5% in the least-exposed by March 2026. The gap is real; AI causation and layoffs are not established.

summary: French permanent hires of 21–29-year-olds fell 28.3% in the most AI-exposed occupations versus 7.5% in the least-exposed; contract endings also fell.
Anthropic reports junior roles fell from 27% to 9% of its technical hires while technical hiring grew in absolute terms.
Neither source identifies AI-caused job loss or predicts an individual outcome.
Yale’s broad U.S. tracker still finds no clear economy-wide AI labor-market footprint.
Yale Budget Lab’s October update still finds no clear U.S. AI labor-market footprint in broad occupational, use and exposure checks; it does not settle narrower risks.
A U.S. working paper identifies 6.1 million workers in high-AI-exposure occupations with low average transition capacity; no AI-caused layoffs were counted.
uncertainty: The French analysis is descriptive and its flows do not measure age-by-occupation employment stocks.
Anthropic is one rapidly growing firm reporting internal, non-audited records.
The Copilot studies use different firm samples and hiring denominators; neither establishes an economy-wide effect.
The adaptive-capacity study combines occupation-level exposure and transition proxies, not observed AI layoffs or realized reemployment.
Occupation averages conceal individual circumstances; future demand may change the ranking.
A new German journal abstract covers mostly pre-generative-AI adoption; its full methods were not accessible.
The sector study uses task exposure rather than observed AI deployment and adjusts a pre-trend in its automatable-task series.
The Argentine experiment took place outside workplaces and did not test actual job access or wages.
The Swedish AI-skill study covers 2014–2023 external hires and excludes ordinary chatbot use; its observational pay gap cannot identify a causal return to training.
The October tracker summary did not expose its full updated data vintage or detailed estimates in the page inspected.
freshness_note: Checked 21 October 2026. French hiring-flow and Anthropic internal evidence sharpen the entry-level warning but do not establish AI-caused unemployment.
